source: Cambodia Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF), "ប្រព័ន្ធវប្បកម្មដំណាំស្រូវ តាមគោលការណ៍ធម្មជាតិ (ប.វ.ស)" [System of Rice Intensification Following Natural Principles / SRI], 14-page Khmer-language handout/booklet, undated, no author or elibrary URL visible on any page (footer reads "កំរណ៉ការអភិវ័ទ្ធន៍វិស្ស័យកសិកម្ម ខែត្តកំពងចាម" = "Agricultural Extension/Skills Development Office, Kampong Cham province")
text:
The source document states five core agronomic principles behind SRI (System of Rice Intensification):

1. Rice is not an aquatic plant, but it is water-tolerant. When rice grows in shallow/minimal standing water rather than deep flooding, its growth potential and its ability to tiller are better.

2. Rice's natural tillering potential declines if the seedling is transplanted after it is more than 15 days old; younger seedlings retain higher tillering capacity.

3. Rice will show higher tillering potential if damage/stress to the roots is minimized at transplanting -- for example, by using a transplanting method that avoids injuring the roots when seedlings are pulled from the nursery bed, rather than letting them sit bundled for a long period before replanting.

4. If rice is transplanted as a single seedling per hill (rather than several seedlings clumped together), the plant will grow and tiller according to its own full natural potential, without competing against other seedlings sharing the same hill.

5. Rice grows best when the soil has good aeration (air/oxygen exchange) and adequate nutrient availability, rather than being kept waterlogged, which restricts root oxygen.

These five principles are the stated rationale for the specific SRI techniques (young single-seedling transplanting, wide spacing, alternating wet-dry water management, and frequent soil aeration/weeding) described elsewhere in the same document.
